name: 9th Grade Success Package
description: Help 9th graders succeed across typical freshman material: Algebra I, English 9, Biology, world history and geography, plus study skills, tests, and projects.
longDescription: A full freshman-year package for typical 9th grade courses. Students get study habits, Algebra I (equations, graphs, systems, polynomials), English 9 (reading, thesis, evidence, grammar), Biology (cells, genetics, ecosystems), world history and geography, and coaching for tests and projects. Clear, encouraging, and focused on understanding — not copying graded work.
primaryGoal: Help 9th grade students keep up with core classes, study with a plan, and build habits that last through high school.
disclaimer: For learning and practice only. Follow your school's honor code — this coach helps you understand ideas, not copy answers on graded work. Do not share personal information (full name, school address, passwords) in Ask. Talk to a parent, teacher, or counselor for serious academic or personal concerns.

capabilities.title: Learn
capabilities.description: Follow modules on study skills and typical 9th grade subjects.

capabilities.title: Ask
capabilities.description: Get help understanding topics and study strategies.

capabilities.title: Scenarios
capabilities.description: Practice planning and school decisions with fictional situations.

capabilities.title: Quiz
capabilities.description: Check study skills and core 9th grade subject basics.

systemPrompt: You are the 9th Grade Success Package coach inside Guardian — a supportive tutor for high school freshmen (about age 14–15). Help students succeed in typical 9th grade courses: Algebra I (linear equations, inequalities, graphing, systems, exponents, polynomials), English 9 (reading literature, thesis, evidence, grammar, MLA), Biology (cells, scientific method, genetics, photosynthesis, ecosystems), and world history/geography (sources, timelines, maps, cause and effect). Also coach weekly planning, notes, test prep, and projects. Use clear, encouraging language — respectful and not childish. Break problems into steps. Teach the process; give hints before full solutions on practice problems. For assigned homework the student must turn in, do NOT provide final answers to copy — guide with questions, similar examples, and the next step. Promote academic integrity and asking teachers for help. Never collect personal details. If a topic is beyond 9th grade, say so briefly and offer a simpler foundation. Schools vary — if their class uses Geometry or Earth Science instead, still help at a 9th-grade level. Encourage breaks, sleep, and talking to adults when stressed.
responseRules: Use short paragraphs and numbered steps when explaining.
Match a freshman reading level; define new terms simply.
On graded assignments, coach understanding — do not write submissions for the student.
Use fresh practice examples rather than reproducing textbook copyright content.
Celebrate effort and good study habits, not just correct answers.
Suggest using their Guardian student vault and Gideon for their own notes and due dates.
starterQuestions: How should I study for a biology test?
How do I write a thesis statement for an essay?
How do I solve a system of two equations?
What is the difference between genotype and phenotype?
I have two tests and a project due — how do I plan my week?

roadmap.title: Freshman Study Skills
roadmap.description: Habits that make 9th grade manageable from week one.
learningObjectives: Use a simple weekly planning routine
Take notes you can actually review
Ask teachers for help before you fall behind

roadmap.title: Algebra I
roadmap.description: Equations, graphs, systems, and polynomials — show your work.
learningObjectives: Solve linear equations and check answers
Tackle inequalities, systems, exponents, and basic polynomials

roadmap.title: English 9
roadmap.description: Reading, thesis-driven writing, evidence, and sentence control.
learningObjectives: Write a clear thesis and body paragraphs with evidence
Annotate literature for theme, character, and craft
Fix run-ons, fragments, and citation basics

roadmap.title: Biology
roadmap.description: Cells, genetics, energy, and ecosystems with the scientific method.
learningObjectives: Explain cell parts and the scientific method

roadmap.title: World History & Geography
roadmap.description: Evidence, maps, timelines, and cause-and-effect writing.
learningObjectives: Tell primary sources from secondary sources
Use maps and timelines for context

roadmap.title: Tests & Projects
roadmap.description: Prepare for exams and longer assignments without cramming.
learningObjectives: Manage test-day stress with simple strategies

knowledgeTopics.title: Planning Your Week
knowledgeTopics.summary: A simple plan beats cramming — map deadlines first, then study in small blocks.
details: List every due date from syllabi, classroom boards, or your planner app.
Work backward: start projects at least a few days before they are due.
Study in 25–40 minute blocks with short breaks (Pomodoro-style).
Do the hardest subject when you have the most energy, not at midnight.
Keep one place for school tasks — paper planner or app — and check it daily.

examples.title: Thursday biology quiz
examples.description: Review notes Monday (15 min), practice questions Tuesday, quick recap Wednesday — instead of one stressed hour Wednesday night.

keyPoints: Small daily sessions beat marathon cramming
commonMistakes: Only writing homework due tomorrow and missing long-term projects
Multitasking with social media during study blocks
starterQuestions: How do I plan when everything is due the same week?
What is a good study block length?

knowledgeTopics.title: Notes That Help Later
knowledgeTopics.summary: Good notes are short, organized, and reviewed — not a transcript of every word the teacher says.
details: Write the date, class, and topic at the top of each page.
Capture main ideas, definitions, and examples — skip filler words.
Leave margin space for questions or labels (Cornell-style: cues on the left, notes on the right).
Review notes within 24 hours for five minutes — it locks in memory.
Star or highlight what the teacher repeated or put on the board.

examples.title: Biology cell unit
examples.description: One page: organelle names, one job each, one drawing — better than copying every slide word for word.

keyPoints: Ask questions in the margin when confused
commonMistakes: Never rereading notes until the night before the test
Trying to write every word instead of main ideas
starterQuestions: What should I write down in class?
How do I study from my notes?

knowledgeTopics.title: Staying Caught Up in 9th Grade
knowledgeTopics.summary: High school moves faster — small daily habits beat catching up after a bad week.
details: Check the syllabus and learning platform (Google Classroom, Canvas, etc.) every school day.
If you miss a class, get notes and the assignment the same day — not the night before the quiz.
Ask your teacher during or right after class when something is unclear; office hours exist for a reason.
Keep a simple homework folder (paper or digital) so nothing lives only in a locker or a chat thread.
Protect sleep: most freshmen need about 8–10 hours. Tired brains forget formulas and essay plans.

examples.title: Missed algebra
examples.description: Email or message: 'I was absent Tuesday — what should I complete before Thursday's quiz?' Attach what you already tried.

keyPoints: Ask early, not the night before
commonMistakes: Waiting until Sunday to open the class site
Assuming 'I'll remember it' without writing the due date down
starterQuestions: What should I do if I missed class?
How do I talk to a teacher when I am confused?

knowledgeTopics.title: Algebra I Basics
knowledgeTopics.summary: Freshman algebra builds on equations, graphing, and patterns — step-by-step work matters more than speed.
details: Two-step equations: undo addition/subtraction first, then multiplication/division.
Keep equations balanced — do the same operation to both sides.
Graph linear equations in slope-intercept form y = mx + b (m = slope, b = y-intercept).
Word problems: define a variable, write an equation, check if the answer makes sense.
Show your work so you can find mistakes and earn partial credit.

examples.title: Solve 3x + 5 = 20
examples.description: Subtract 5 from both sides → 3x = 15 → divide by 3 → x = 5. Check: 3(5) + 5 = 20.

keyPoints: Practice similar problems, not just watching videos
commonMistakes: Skipping steps and losing track of negative signs
Memorizing answers without understanding the method
starterQuestions: How do I solve a two-step equation?
What is slope in a graph?

knowledgeTopics.title: Inequalities & Systems
knowledgeTopics.summary: Inequalities use the same inverse operations as equations — flip the inequality if you multiply or divide by a negative. Systems ask where two lines meet.
details: Solve inequalities like equations; graph the solution on a number line (open circle for < or >, closed for ≤ or ≥).
When you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign.
A system of two linear equations can be solved by graphing, substitution, or elimination.
Substitution: solve one equation for a variable, plug into the other.
Check by plugging both values back into both original equations.
keyPoints: Flip the sign only for negative multiply/divide
A solution to a system works in both equations
commonMistakes: Forgetting to reverse the inequality
Finding x but never solving for y
starterQuestions: When do I flip an inequality?
How do I solve a system by substitution?

knowledgeTopics.title: Exponents & Polynomials
knowledgeTopics.summary: Exponent rules keep powers organized; polynomials are sums of terms like 3x² + 2x − 5.
details: Product rule: x^a · x^b = x^(a+b). Quotient: x^a / x^b = x^(a−b). Power: (x^a)^b = x^(ab).
x^0 = 1 (for x ≠ 0). Negative exponents mean reciprocals: x^(−n) = 1/x^n.
Combine like terms: 4x² + 3x² = 7x². You cannot combine 4x² and 3x.
Distribute: 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10. FOIL for (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 5x + 6.
Factor when you can pull out a GCF: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3).
keyPoints: Add exponents when multiplying the same base
commonMistakes: Adding bases instead of exponents (2³ · 2² is not 4^5)
Combining 3x² and 3x
starterQuestions: What is the product rule for exponents?
How do I multiply two binomials?

knowledgeTopics.title: English 9 Reading & Writing
knowledgeTopics.summary: Essays need a clear thesis, organized paragraphs, and evidence from the text.
details: Thesis = your main argument in one sentence (what you are proving).
Body paragraphs: topic sentence → evidence (quote or example) → explain how it supports the thesis.
When reading, annotate: underline key lines, note character motives and themes.
Revise for clarity: read aloud, cut repeated words, fix run-on sentences.
Cite sources and quotes the way your teacher asks (MLA is common in 9th grade).

examples.title: Literary analysis
examples.description: Thesis: The protagonist's choices show growing responsibility. Each paragraph uses one scene from the book as evidence.

keyPoints: Draft early so you can revise
commonMistakes: Summarizing the plot without analyzing
Quotes dropped in without explaining them
starterQuestions: How do I write a thesis?
How long should a body paragraph be?

knowledgeTopics.title: Reading Literature
knowledgeTopics.summary: 9th grade English asks what a text means and how the author built that meaning — not only what happened.
details: Track characters: what they want, what they fear, how they change.
Theme is a message about life the story suggests — not just the topic (love vs. 'jealousy destroys trust').
Notice craft: imagery, symbolism, irony, point of view, and how dialogue reveals character.
Annotate: short margin notes on 'why this line matters,' not only highlights.
For poetry, read aloud once, then look at line breaks, repetition, and the turn (shift) in meaning.

examples.title: Theme vs plot
examples.description: Plot: a student lies about a test. Theme might be: honesty is harder than the short-term fix, but it rebuilds trust.

keyPoints: Theme is a full idea, not one word
commonMistakes: Retelling the whole plot instead of analyzing a few key moments
Calling the topic (war, family) the theme
starterQuestions: How do I find the theme of a story?
What should I annotate while I read?

knowledgeTopics.title: Sentences & Citations
knowledgeTopics.summary: Clear sentences and honest citations make essays readable and keep you in honor-code territory.
details: A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb and a complete thought. Fragments are missing one of those.
Run-ons smash two sentences together. Fix with a period, semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS).
Keep verb tense consistent unless time actually changes in the story.
MLA in-text: author and page, like (Lee 23). Works Cited lists full sources.
Paraphrase still needs a citation if the idea is not yours. Quotes need quotation marks plus a citation.

examples.title: Fix a run-on
examples.description: Wrong: The narrator is afraid she still goes outside. Right: The narrator is afraid, but she still goes outside.

keyPoints: One complete thought per sentence (or join them correctly)
Read drafts aloud to catch errors
commonMistakes: Comma splices (comma only between two full sentences)
Dropping a quote with no page or explanation
starterQuestions: How do I fix a run-on sentence?
When do I need an MLA citation?

knowledgeTopics.title: Biology Foundations
knowledgeTopics.summary: 9th grade biology often starts with cells, organization of life, and ecosystems — vocabulary and diagrams go together.
details: Cell theory: all living things are made of cells; cells come from cells.
Know major organelles and jobs (nucleus, mitochondria, cell membrane, etc.).
Scientific method: question, hypothesis, experiment, data, conclusion.
Ecosystems: producers, consumers, decomposers; energy flows, matter cycles.
Use labeled drawings and flashcards for terms — spelling counts on tests.

examples.title: Mitochondria
examples.description: Often called the powerhouse of the cell — where cellular respiration releases energy (ATP) for the cell to use.

keyPoints: Practice explaining processes in your own words
commonMistakes: Memorizing definitions without understanding function
Ignoring lab safety and procedure questions on tests
starterQuestions: What are the main parts of a cell?
How does the scientific method work?

knowledgeTopics.title: Genetics Basics
knowledgeTopics.summary: DNA carries instructions; genes are segments of DNA; traits show up through dominant and recessive alleles.
details: DNA → genes → proteins → traits (a simplified chain you will see on quizzes).
Alleles are versions of a gene. Dominant alleles can mask recessive ones in the phenotype.
Genotype is the allele pair (Bb); phenotype is what you observe (brown eyes, if B is brown).
Punnett squares predict probable offspring genotypes — they are not guarantees for one child.
Homozygous means two of the same allele (BB or bb); heterozygous means two different (Bb).

examples.title: Punnett square
examples.description: Cross Bb × Bb. Offspring genotypes: 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb. If B is dominant, 3/4 show the dominant phenotype.

keyPoints: Learn the vocabulary with a tiny sketch
commonMistakes: Thinking a 3:1 ratio means the next child must be dominant
Mixing up gene, DNA, and chromosome
starterQuestions: What is the difference between genotype and phenotype?
How do I fill in a Punnett square?

knowledgeTopics.title: Energy, Photosynthesis & Ecosystems
knowledgeTopics.summary: Plants capture light energy; food webs pass energy (with losses) from producers to consumers.
details: Photosynthesis: plants use light, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar and oxygen.
Cellular respiration releases energy (ATP) from sugar — happens in plants and animals.
Producers make their own food; consumers eat others; decomposers recycle matter.
Energy pyramids: only about 10% of energy typically moves up each trophic level — the rest is used or lost as heat.
Matter cycles (carbon, water, nitrogen); energy flows one way through the ecosystem.

examples.title: Food chain
examples.description: Grass (producer) → rabbit (primary consumer) → fox (secondary). Most energy is not passed to the fox.

keyPoints: Photosynthesis stores energy; respiration releases it
Labels on diagrams matter on tests
commonMistakes: Saying energy is recycled the same way as carbon
Skipping units and arrows on lab graphs
starterQuestions: What do plants need for photosynthesis?
Why are there fewer hawks than rabbits in a food web?

knowledgeTopics.title: History & Civics Basics
knowledgeTopics.summary: History class is about evidence and context — dates matter, but so does why events happened.
details: Primary sources = from the time period; secondary sources = later analysis.
Timelines help you see cause and effect across events.
Short essays: claim, evidence from documents, reasoning linking evidence to claim.
Compare perspectives — whose voice is included or missing?
Study maps, key terms, and big themes your teacher emphasized in class.

examples.title: Document-based question
examples.description: Use at least two sources to support your answer; explain how each source supports your claim.

commonMistakes: Listing facts without explaining significance
Using only one document in a multi-source prompt
starterQuestions: What is a primary source?
How do I study for a history test?

knowledgeTopics.title: Maps, Regions & Context
knowledgeTopics.summary: Geography explains where events happen and why place (rivers, trade routes, climate) shapes history.
details: Read map keys, scale, and compass rose before you interpret a map.
Physical maps show landforms; political maps show borders; thematic maps show a topic (population, resources).
Ask: how did mountains, rivers, or coastlines help or limit a civilization?
Regions group places by shared features (climate, language, culture) — borders are often messy.
Pair maps with timelines: the same river valley can matter in different centuries for different reasons.

examples.title: River valley
examples.description: Farming near a river often meant surplus food, cities, and trade — and also floods that societies had to manage.

keyPoints: Place is part of cause and effect
Compare two maps from different times
commonMistakes: Memorizing names with no idea where they are
Ignoring the map title and thinking every map is the same type
starterQuestions: How do I read a historical map?
Why do rivers show up so often in world history?

knowledgeTopics.title: Studying for Tests
knowledgeTopics.summary: Active review — practice questions, flashcards, teaching aloud — beats rereading the chapter once.
details: Start three to five days early for unit tests when possible.
Make a one-page cheat sheet of formulas, terms, and big ideas (even if you cannot use it on test day, making it helps).
Practice problems for math; practice questions for science and history.
Sleep well the night before — all-nighters hurt recall.
Read test directions carefully; answer easy questions first to build confidence.

examples.title: Active recall
examples.description: Cover definitions and try to say them aloud before peeking — stronger than highlighting everything.

keyPoints: Arrive prepared with materials your teacher allows
commonMistakes: Only rereading the textbook
Studying new material the morning of the test instead of reviewing
starterQuestions: How do I study for a math test?
What should I do the night before an exam?

knowledgeTopics.title: Projects & Long Assignments
knowledgeTopics.summary: Big assignments need milestones — research, outline, draft, revise — not one panic session.
details: Read the rubric first; highlight what gets the most points.
Break the project into steps with mini-deadlines before the final due date.
Research: use trusted sources; track where each fact came from.
Outline before drafting essays or slide decks.
Leave time for proofreading and asking a teacher or peer to review.

examples.title: Research paper
examples.description: Week 1: topic and sources. Week 2: outline. Week 3: draft. Week 4: revise and submit.

keyPoints: Revision is part of the grade
commonMistakes: Starting the night before
Ignoring citation requirements until the end
starterQuestions: How do I start a research project?
What goes in an essay outline?

glossary.definition: The main argument or claim of an essay, usually one sentence in the introduction.
In a line equation y = mx + b, m is the slope — how steep the line is.
A grid that shows possible allele combinations from two parents and the probability of each genotype.
The process plants use to turn light, water, and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen.
Two or more equations considered together; the solution is the pair (or set) of values that works in all of them.
A message about life suggested by a story or poem — more than a one-word topic.
A common citation style in English class: short in-text citations plus a Works Cited list.
A document or artifact from the time period being studied.
A testable prediction in a science experiment.
Studying by trying to remember information without looking — then checking answers.
A scoring guide that shows what teachers expect on an assignment.

quizzes.title: Study Skills Quiz
quizzes.description: Check your planning and note-taking basics.

questions.question: What is usually the best way to prepare for a test on Friday?
options: Study only Thursday night for four hours
Review in short sessions across several days
Reread the chapter once without practicing
questions.explanation: Spreading study over days with active practice improves memory more than one cram session.

questions.question: Good notes should capture every word the teacher says.
questions.explanation: Focus on main ideas, definitions, and examples — not a full transcript.

questions.question: When you are stuck on homework you must turn in, what should you do first?
options: Copy the full answer from an AI tool
Try the next step, use hints, then ask your teacher
questions.explanation: Understanding matters — use hints and teacher help while following your school's honor code.

quizzes.title: 9th Grade Subject Basics
quizzes.description: Quick check on math, English, science, and history foundations.

questions.question: In y = 2x + 3, what is the slope?
questions.explanation: In slope-intercept form y = mx + b, the coefficient of x (m) is the slope.

questions.question: Which is a primary source?
options: A textbook chapter written in 2020 about the Civil War
A letter written by a soldier during the Civil War
A study guide made by your teacher
questions.explanation: Primary sources come from the time period; textbooks and later articles are secondary.

questions.question: The mitochondria is often described as the powerhouse of the cell.
questions.explanation: Mitochondria produce ATP through cellular respiration — energy for the cell.

questions.question: What belongs in a strong body paragraph?
options: Only a quote with no explanation
A brand-new thesis unrelated to the essay
Only the plot summary of the book
questions.explanation: Each paragraph should support the thesis with evidence and your analysis.

questions.question: Solve 4x − 6 = 10. What is x?
questions.explanation: Add 6 to both sides → 4x = 16 → divide by 4 → x = 4. Check: 4(4) − 6 = 10.

questions.question: When you multiply both sides of an inequality by a negative number, you reverse the inequality sign.
questions.explanation: That flip is required so the inequality still describes the same set of numbers.

questions.question: x² · x³ equals
questions.explanation: Product rule: add exponents when the bases are the same — 2 + 3 = 5.

questions.question: Which is the best description of a thesis?
options: The main argument you will prove in the essay
A quote from the book with no explanation
The last sentence of the story
questions.explanation: A thesis is a claim the rest of the essay supports with evidence.

questions.question: A run-on can be fixed with a period or with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction.
questions.explanation: You can also use a semicolon. A comma alone is a comma splice — not enough.

questions.question: Theme is best described as
options: A message about life the text suggests
questions.explanation: Theme is an idea the work explores, not just the subject matter.

questions.question: Genotype refers to
questions.explanation: Genotype is the alleles (e.g. Bb). Phenotype is what you see.

questions.question: Photosynthesis uses light, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar and oxygen.
questions.explanation: That is the core process 9th grade biology expects you to state and label.

questions.question: In a typical energy pyramid, as you move to higher trophic levels, available energy
questions.explanation: Energy is used or lost as heat; only a fraction moves up. Matter cycles; energy flows.

questions.question: A political map mainly shows
questions.explanation: Political maps emphasize countries, cities, and borders; physical maps emphasize landforms.

questions.question: A diary written during the time you are studying is usually a primary source.
questions.explanation: Primary sources come from the period; later textbooks are secondary.

scenarios.title: Busy Week Planning
scenarios.context: It is Sunday. You have a math test Wednesday, a history project due Friday, and regular homework each night. You also have soccer practice Tuesday and Thursday.
scenarios.question: What is the smartest first step?
choices: Ignore the project until Thursday night
List all deadlines and block study time before Wednesday and around practice
Study only your favorite subject all week
scenarios.explanation: Listing deadlines and scheduling short study blocks — especially before the math test — protects both grades and activities.
learningPoints: Plan around fixed events like practice
Math test prep should begin before Tuesday night

scenarios.title: Stuck on Graded Homework
scenarios.notice: Practice making good choices about academic integrity.
scenarios.context: You are stuck on problem 7 of tonight's algebra homework. It will be collected tomorrow for a grade.
scenarios.question: What is the best approach?
choices: Paste the full solution from the internet
Identify where you got lost, try a similar example, ask for a hint, then visit office hours or email your teacher
Leave it blank and hope for extra credit
scenarios.explanation: Learn the method with hints and teacher support — that builds skills and follows honor code expectations.
learningPoints: Partial work with effort often earns partial credit
Teachers expect questions when you are stuck
Copying undermines learning and can have serious consequences

scenarios.title: English Essay Week
scenarios.context: Your English 9 essay is due Friday. You have read the book but have not written a thesis. Soccer is Tuesday and Thursday.
scenarios.question: What is the strongest plan?
choices: Write the whole essay Thursday after practice
Draft a thesis and outline Monday, write a body paragraph Tuesday, revise Wednesday, proofread Thursday
Copy a sample essay from the internet and change a few words
Skip soccer for the rest of the year
scenarios.explanation: Breaking writing into thesis, draft, and revise beats one late night — and keeps academic integrity.

scenarios.title: Biology Lab Confusion
scenarios.context: Your photosynthesis lab graph does not match the class average. The lab is graded on method, data, and a written conclusion.
scenarios.question: What should you do?
choices: Change your numbers so they match the class
Report your real data, check your units and procedure, and explain possible error in the conclusion
Copy a lab from last year's student
scenarios.explanation: Science values honest data plus reasoning. Unexpected results can still earn credit if you explain method and error.

interviewQuestions.question: Describe a study routine that would help you before a big test.
answerGuide: Start early, not the night before only
Use active recall or practice problems
Adjust based on what the test covers
followUpQuestions: Which subject needs the most time in your routine?
What distracts you most when studying?

interviewQuestions.question: Explain how you would check that x = 4 is the solution to 3x + 2 = 14.
answerGuide: If it does not, redo the inverse operations
followUpQuestions: What would you try if the check failed?
How do you keep negative signs from disappearing?

interviewQuestions.question: What makes a strong thesis for a literary analysis essay?
answerGuide: It is a claim, not just a topic
It can be supported with quotes
It is specific enough to prove in a few paragraphs
It is not a plot summary
followUpQuestions: How would you turn 'friendship' into a thesis?
Where does the thesis usually appear?
